idiom_name: typed MessageStore interface + prepared statement behind one row mapper
implementation_notes: TypeScript's contribution is the contract: a MessageRecord interface (plus a union when payload shapes vary) with the store behind a MessageStore interface whose append/byCorrelation/purgeBefore methods are the only way in, so the record schema, the retention policy and every writing call site are checked by the compiler - the classic Store abstraction survives as a type rather than as a class hierarchy. The implementation is Node's SQLite binding (node:sqlite DatabaseSync or better-sqlite3) with a prepared statement, and all column-to-object conversion lives in one row mapper so the SQL schema and the interface cannot drift apart unnoticed. The tap is a queue or worker flush as in JavaScript, and tests substitute an in-memory implementation of the same interface. A hand-written class hierarchy with pluggable backends is still justified when several stores must be selected at runtime; for one audit database the interface plus the mapper is the pattern.
pitfalls: Types stop at the schema: the SQL and the interface drift unless one row mapper is the single place where columns become MessageRecord; keep it and test it.
node:sqlite is version-gated and better-sqlite3 is a native addon, so the binding belongs behind the interface - otherwise deployments that cannot load it fail to compile or test.
A synchronous prepared statement inside an async handler blocks the event loop, exactly as in JavaScript; the tap must be a queue or a worker.
Optional fields (correlationId?) become NULL columns: reporting queries must not assume their presence, and indexes on mostly-NULL columns rarely help.
